Self-adjointness of a generalized Camassa-Holm equation
N.H. Ibragimov, R.S. Khamitova

Department of Mathematics and Science,
Blekinge Institute of Technology,
SE-371 79 Karlskrona, Sweden
and

A. Valenti

Department of Mathematics and Computer Sciences,
University of Catania, I 95125 Catania, Italy

Abstract
It is well known that the Camassa-Holm equation possesses numerous remarkable properties characteristic for KdV type equations. In this paper we show that it shares one more property with the KdV equation. Namely, it is shown in [1, 2] that the KdV and the modified KdV equations are self-adjoint. Starting from the generalization [3] of the Camassa-Holm equation [4], we prove that the Camassa-Holm equation is self-adjoint. This property is important, e.g. for constructing conservation laws associated with symmetries of the equation in question. Accordingly, we construct conservation laws for the generalized Camassa-Holm equation using its symmetries.

Keywords: Camassa-Holm equation, Quasi self-adjointness, Conservation laws.

AMS classification numbers: 35C99, 35G20, 35L65, 22E70, 35Q35, 35Q51

1 Introduction

The Camassa-Holm equation

F≡ut−ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−2​ux​ux​x+3​u​ux+κ​ux=0F\equiv u_{t}-u_{txx}-u\,u_{xxx}-2\,u_{x}u_{xx}+3\,u\,u_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}=0 (1)

has appeared in [4], [5] as a shallow water wave equation. Here u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is the fluid velocity in the xx direction and κ\kappa is an arbitrary constant. Eq. (1) was studied also by Fokas [6] and Fuchsstainer [7].

Clarkson, Mansfield and Priestley [3] studied the third-order nonlinear equation of the form

F≡ut−ϵ​ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−β​ux​ux​x−α​u​ux+κ​ux=0F\equiv u_{t}-\epsilon\,u_{txx}-u\,u_{xxx}-\beta\,u_{x}u_{xx}-\alpha\,u\,u_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}=0 (2)

with arbitrary parameters ϵ,α,β.\epsilon,\,\alpha,\,\beta. It contains not only the Camassa-Holm equation (1) as a particular case, but also other interesting nonlinear equations such as:

  • •

    the Fornberg-Whitham equation [8]

    ut−ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−3​ux​ux​x+u​ux+ux=0,u_{t}-\,u_{txx}-u\,u_{xxx}-3\,u_{x}u_{xx}+u\,u_{x}+u_{x}=0,
  • •

    the Rosenau-Hyman equation [9]

    ut−u​ux​x​x−3​ux​ux​x−u​ux=0.u_{t}-u\,u_{xxx}-3\,u_{x}u_{xx}-u\,u_{x}=0.

Eq. (1), as any evolution type equation, does not have a usual Lagrangian11 1 By this we mean that there is no function L⁡(x,t,u,ux,ut,ux​x,ut​x,…)L(x,t,u,u_{x},u_{t},u_{xx},u_{tx},\ldots) such that Eq. (1) is identical with the Euler-Lagrange equation δ​Lδ​u≡∂L∂u−Dx​∂L∂ux−Dt​∂L∂ut+Dx2​∂L∂ux​x+Dt​Dx​∂L∂ut​x+⋯=0.\frac{\delta L}{\delta u}\equiv\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}-D_{x}\frac{\partial L}{\partial u_{x}}-D_{t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial u_{t}}+D_{x}^{2}\frac{\partial L}{\partial u_{xx}}+D_{t}D_{x}\frac{\partial L}{\partial u_{tx}}+\cdots=0. However it is shown in [10] that the CH equation can be written as the Euler-Poincaré equation. It also admits two canonical Hamiltonian representations, namely in terms of the Clebsch variables and the so-called peakon variables, obtained by using different momentum maps.. Therefore the classical Noether theorem cannot be employed for constructing conservation laws using symmetries of Eq. (1). On the other hand, a new procedure was developed in [2] for constructing conservations laws associated with symmetries. The new procedure allows one to construct a conservation law using any (Lie point, Lie-Bäcklund, nonlocal, etc.) symmetry of any differential equation. However, the resulting conservation laws involve, in general, not only the solutions of the original equation, but also so-called nonlocal variables, namely solutions of the adjoint equation. The nonlocal variables can be eliminated if the equation under consideration is quasi self-adjoint (or, in particular, self-adjoint) in the sense defined in [11]. Therefore the quasi self-adjointness is important for constructing conservation laws. Accordingly, we start our paper with investigating the quasi self-adjointness of the generalized Camassa-Holm equation (2). Our construction require the concepts of the formal Lagrangian and the adjoint equation for Eq. (2).

2 Formal Lagrangian and adjoint equation

According to the procedure suggested in [2], we introduce the formal Lagrangian

ℒ≡v​F=v⁡[ut−ϵ​ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−β​ux​ux​x−α​u​ux+κ​ux]{\cal{L}}\equiv vF=v\left[u_{t}-\epsilon\,u_{txx}-uu_{xxx}-\beta\,u_{x}u_{xx}-\alpha\,uu_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}\right] (3)

and define the adjoint equation F∗=0F^{*}=0 by

F∗≡δ​ℒδ​u=0.F^{*}\equiv\frac{\delta{\cal{L}}}{\delta u}=0. (4)

Here v=v⁡(t,x)v=v(t,x) is a new dependent variable,

δδ​u=∂∂u−Di​∂∂ui+Di​Dj​∂∂ui​j−Di​Dj​Dk​∂∂ui​j​k+…(i,j,k=1,2),\frac{\delta}{\delta u}=\frac{\partial}{\partial u}-D_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{i}}+D_{i}D_{j}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{ij}}-D_{i}D_{j}D_{k}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{ijk}}+...\qquad(i,j,k=1,2),

is the variational derivative and

Di=∂∂xi+ui​∂∂u+vi​∂∂v+ui​j​∂∂uj+vi​j​∂∂vj+ui​j​k​∂∂uj​k+vi​j​k​∂∂vj​k+…D_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i}}+u_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}+v_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial v}+u_{ij}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{j}}+v_{ij}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_{j}}+u_{ijk}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{jk}}+v_{ijk}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_{jk}}+...

is the operator of total differentiation with respect to xix^{i} (OPENx1=t,x2=x).x^{1}=t,\,x^{2}=x). The usual convention of summation over repeated indices is used.

We have

F∗≡∂ℒ∂u−Dt​∂ℒ∂ut−Dx​∂ℒ∂ux+Dx2​∂ℒ∂ux​x−Dx3​∂ℒ∂ux​x​x−Dt​Dx2​∂ℒ∂ut​x​x=0F^{*}\equiv\frac{\partial\cal{L}}{\partial u}-D_{t}\frac{\partial\cal{L}}{\partial u_{t}}-D_{x}\frac{\partial\cal{L}}{\partial u_{x}}+D_{x}^{2}\frac{\partial\cal{L}}{\partial u_{xx}}-D_{x}^{3}\frac{\partial\cal{L}}{\partial u_{xxx}}-D_{t}D_{x}^{2}\frac{\partial\cal{L}}{\partial u_{txx}}=0 (5)

and, taking into account the relation (3), we obtain

F∗=\displaystyle F^{*}= −\displaystyle- v​ux​x​x−α​v​ux−Dt​(v)−Dx​(−β​v​ux​x−α​v​u+κ​v)\displaystyle vu_{xxx}-\alpha\,vu_{x}-D_{t}(v)-D_{x}(-\beta\,vu_{xx}-\alpha\,vu+\kappa\,v)
+\displaystyle+ Dx2​(−β​v​ux)−Dx3​(−v​u)+ϵ​Dt​Dx2​(v).\displaystyle D_{x}^{2}(-\beta\,vu_{x})-D_{x}^{3}(-vu)+\epsilon\,D_{t}D_{x}^{2}(v).

Performing here the differentiations, we arrive at the following adjoint Eq. (4):

F∗≡−vt+ϵ​vt​x​x+u​vx​x​x+(3−β)​(ux​vx​x−vx​ux​x)+α​u​vx−κ​vx=0.F^{*}\equiv-v_{t}+\epsilon\,v_{txx}+uv_{xxx}+(3-\beta)(u_{x}v_{xx}-v_{x}u_{xx})+\alpha\,uv_{x}-\kappa\,v_{x}=0. (6)

Definition 1. An equation F=0F=0 is said to be quasi self-adjoint [11] if there exists a function

v=φ⁡(u),φ′​(u)≠0,v=\varphi(u),\quad\varphi^{\prime}(u)\neq 0, (7)

such that

F∗∣v=φ⁡(u)=λ​FF^{*}\mid_{v=\varphi(u)}=\lambda\,F (8)

with an undetermined coefficient λ\lambda. If in (7) φ⁡(u)=u,\varphi(u)=u, we say that the equation F=0F=0 is self-adjoint.

Taking into account the expression (6) of F∗F^{*} and using Eq. (7) together with its consequences

vt=φ′​ut,vx=φ′​ux,v_{t}=\varphi^{\prime}u_{t},\quad v_{x}=\varphi^{\prime}u_{x},
vt​x=φ′​ut​x+φ′′​ut​ux,vx​x=φ′​ux​x+φ′′​ux2,v_{tx}=\varphi^{\prime}u_{tx}+\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{t}u_{x},\quad v_{xx}=\varphi^{\prime}u_{xx}+\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{x}^{2},
vt​x​x=φ′​ut​x​x+2​φ′′​ux​ut​x+φ′′​ut​ux​x+φ′′′​ut​ux2,v_{txx}=\varphi^{\prime}u_{txx}+2\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{x}u_{tx}+\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{t}u_{xx}+\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}u_{t}u_{x}^{2},
vx​x​x=φ′​ux​x​x+3​φ′′​ux​ux​x+φ′′′​ux3,v_{xxx}=\varphi^{\prime}u_{xxx}+3\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{x}u_{xx}+\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}u_{x}^{3},

we rewrite Eq. (8) in the following form:

−φ′ut+αφ′uux−κφ′ux+[φ′′′u−(β−3)φ′′)]ux3+φ′uux​x​x\displaystyle-\varphi^{\prime}u_{t}+\alpha\,\varphi^{\prime}u\,u_{x}-\kappa\,\varphi^{\prime}u_{x}+[\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}u-(\beta-3)\,\varphi^{\prime\prime})]\,u_{x}^{3}+\varphi^{\prime}u\,u_{xxx}
+ϵφ′ut​x​x+[3φ′′u−2(β−3)φ′)]uxux​x+2ϵφ′′uxut​x+ϵφ′′′utux2\displaystyle+\,\epsilon\,\varphi^{\prime}u_{txx}+\,[3\,\varphi^{\prime\prime}u-2\,(\beta-3)\,\varphi^{\prime})]\,u_{x}\,u_{xx}+2\,\epsilon\,\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{x}\,u_{tx}+\epsilon\,\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}u_{t}\,u_{x}^{2}
+ϵ​φ′′​ut​ux​x=λ⁡(ut−ϵ​ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−α​u​ux−β​ux​ux​x+κ​ux).\displaystyle+\,\epsilon\,\varphi^{\prime\prime}u_{t}\,u_{xx}=\lambda\,(u_{t}-\epsilon\,u_{txx}-uu_{xxx}-\alpha\,uu_{x}-\beta\,u_{x}u_{xx}+\kappa\,u_{x}). (9)

Eq. (9) should be satisfied identically in all variables ut,ux,ux​x,….u_{t},\,u_{x},\,u_{xx},\,\ldots. Comparing the coefficients of utu_{t} in both sides of Eq. (9), we obtain λ=−φ′\lambda=-\varphi^{\prime}. Then we equate the coefficients of ux​ut​xu_{x}u_{tx} and get:

ϵ​φ′′=0.\epsilon\,\varphi^{\prime\prime}=0. (10)

According to Eq. (10), the procedure splits into two cases:

ϵ=0,\displaystyle\epsilon=0, (11)
ϵ≠0,φ′′=0.\displaystyle\epsilon\neq 0,\quad\varphi^{\prime\prime}=0. (12)

In the case (11) we compare the coefficients of ux​ux​xu_{x}\,u_{xx} and arrive at the equation

φ′′​u+(β−2)​φ′=0.\varphi^{\prime\prime}\,u+(\beta-2)\,\varphi^{\prime}=0. (13)

Integrating Eq. (13) we obtain

φ⁡(u)={a+b​uβ−1,β≠1,a+b​ln⁡u,β=1,\displaystyle\varphi(u)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}a+b\,u^{\beta-1},\quad\beta\neq 1,\\ a+b\,\ln u,\quad\beta=1,\end{array}\right.

where aa and bb are arbitrary constants. The coefficients of the other terms in both sides of Eq. (9) are equal due to Eq. (13). Hence we have proved that the equation

ut−u​ux​x​x−β​ux​ux​x−α​u​ux+κ​ux=0u_{t}-u\,u_{xxx}-\beta\,u_{x}u_{xx}-\alpha\,u\,u_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}=0 (17)

is quasi self-adjoint and that the substitution (7) has the form

v={a+b​uβ−1,β≠1,a+b​ln⁡u,β=1.\displaystyle v=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}a+b\,u^{\beta-1},\quad\beta\neq 1,\\ a+b\,\ln u,\quad\beta=1.\end{array}\right.

Now we consider the case (12). In this case the comparison of the coefficients for ux​ux​xu_{x}u_{xx} yields that β=2\beta=2. The coefficients of the other terms in both sides of Eq. (9) are equal. Thus we have proved that the equation

ut−ϵ​ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−2​ux​ux​x−α​u​ux+κ​ux=0u_{t}-\epsilon\,u_{txx}-u\,u_{xxx}-2\,u_{x}u_{xx}-\alpha\,u\,u_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}=0 (21)

is quasi self-adjoint for any parameters ϵ,α,κ\epsilon,\,\alpha,\,\kappa and that the substitution (7) has the following form:

v=a+b​u.v=a+b\,u. (22)

We can take, in particular, a=0a=0 and b=1b=1. Hence Eq. (21) coincides with its adjoint equation after the substitution v=uv=u. According to [1], it means that the generalized Camassa-Holm equation (21) is self-adjoint.

In conclusion of this section we note that the Fornberg-Whitham equation

ut−ut​x​x−u​ux​x​x−3​ux​ux​x+u​ux+ux=0u_{t}-\,u_{txx}-u\,u_{xxx}-3\,u_{x}u_{xx}+u\,u_{x}+u_{x}=0 (23)

is not quasi self-adjoint in the sense of Definition 1.

3 Conservation laws

3.1 General form

We rewrite the formal Lagrangian (3) in the symmetric form

ℒ=v⁡[ut−ϵ3​(ut​x​x+ux​t​x+ux​x​t)−u​ux​x​x−α​ux​ux​x−β​u​ux+κ​ux].{\cal{L}}=v\left[u_{t}-\frac{\epsilon}{3}(u_{txx}+u_{xtx}+u_{xxt})-u\,u_{xxx}-\alpha\,u_{x}u_{xx}-\beta\,u\,u_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}\right]. (24)

Eq. (2) is said to have a nonlocal conservation law if there exits a vector C=(C1,C2)\textbf{C}=(C^{1},C^{2}) satisfying the equation

Dt​(C1)+Dx​(C2)=0D_{t}(C^{1})+D_{x}(C^{2})=0 (25)

on any solution of the system (2), (6). Eq. (2) has a local conservation law if (25) is satisfied on any solution of Eq. (2).

The conserved vector corresponding to an operator

X=ξ1​(t,x,u)​∂∂t+ξ2​(t,x,u)​∂∂x+η⁡(t,x,u)​∂∂uX=\xi^{1}(t,x,u)\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\xi^{2}(t,x,u)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+\eta(t,x,u)\frac{\partial}{\partial u} (26)

admitted by Eq. (2) is obtained by the following formula [2]:

Ci=ξi​ℒ+W⁡[∂ℒ∂ui−Dj​(∂ℒ∂ui​j)+Dj​Dk​(∂ℒ∂ui​j​k)]\displaystyle C^{i}=\xi^{i}{\cal L}+W\left[\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{i}}-D_{j}\left(\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{ij}}\right)+D_{j}D_{k}\left(\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{ijk}}\right)\right]
+Dj​(W)​[∂ℒ∂ui​j−Dk​(∂ℒ∂ui​j​k)]+Dj​Dk​(W)​∂ℒ∂ui​j​k,\displaystyle\qquad\,+\,D_{j}(W)\left[\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{ij}}-D_{k}\left(\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{ijk}}\right)\right]+D_{j}D_{k}(W)\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{ijk}}, (27)

where i,j,k=1,2i,j,k=1,2 and

W=η−ξi​ui.W=\eta-\xi^{i}u_{i}.

We will construct the conserved vectors (27) using the Lie point symmetries (26) of Eq. (2) found in [3].

3.2 Rosenau-Hyman equation

Letting in Eq. (17) α=1,β=3,κ=0\alpha=1,\,\beta=3,\,\kappa=0, we obtain the Rosenau-Hyman equation

ut−u​ux​x​x−3​ux​ux​x−u​ux=0.u_{t}-u\,u_{xxx}-3\,u_{x}u_{xx}-u\,u_{x}=0. (28)

In this case, the formal Lagrangian (24) and the substitution (2) assume the forms

ℒ=v⁡[ut−u​ux​x​x−3​ux​ux​x−u​ux]{\cal{L}}=v\left[u_{t}-uu_{xxx}-3\,u_{x}u_{xx}-uu_{x}\right] (29)

and

v=a+b​u2,v=a+bu^{2}, (30)

respectively. We construct the conservation law associated with the scaling symmetry

X=u∂∂u−t∂∂t⋅X=u\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}-t\,\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\cdot (31)

For this symmetry we have W=u+t​utW=u+t\,u_{t}. Writing the quantities (27) without the term ξi​ℒ\xi^{i}{\cal L} since the Lagrangian ℒ{\cal L} is equal to zero on solutions of Eq. (28) and taking into account the structure of the formal Lagrangian (29), we obtain

C1=W​∂ℒ∂ut,\displaystyle C^{1}=W\,\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{t}}, (32)
C2=W⁡[∂ℒ∂ux−Dx​(∂ℒ∂ux​x)+Dx2​(∂ℒ∂ux​x​x)]\displaystyle C^{2}=W\left[\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{x}}-D_{x}\left(\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{xx}}\right)+D_{x}^{2}\left(\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{xxx}}\right)\right]
+Dx​(W)​[∂ℒ∂ux​x−Dx​(∂ℒ∂ux​x​x)]+Dx2​(W)​∂ℒ∂ux​x​x.\displaystyle\qquad\,+\,D_{x}(W)\left[\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{xx}}-D_{x}\left(\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{xxx}}\right)\right]+D_{x}^{2}(W)\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial u_{xxx}}. (33)

Substituting in (32) and (33) the expression (29) for ℒ{\cal{L}}, we get

C1=v​W,\displaystyle C^{1}=vW, (34)
C2=(−u​v+ux​vx−v​ux​x−u​vx​x)​W\displaystyle C^{2}=\left(-u\,v+u_{x}v_{x}-v\,u_{xx}-u\,v_{xx}\right)W
+(u​vx−2​v​ux)​Dx​(W)−u​v​Dx2​(W).\displaystyle\qquad+\left(u\,v_{x}-2\,v\,u_{x}\right)D_{x}(W)-u\,v\,D_{x}^{2}(W). (35)

Now we substitute in Eq. (34) the expression W=u+t​ut,W=u+t\,u_{t}, eliminate utu_{t} by using Eq. (28) and obtain:

C1=u​v+t​v​(u​ux​x​x+u​ux+3​ux​ux​x)\displaystyle C^{1}=u\,v+t\,v\left(u\,u_{xxx}+u\,u_{x}+3\,u_{x}u_{xx}\right)
=u​v+t​u​v​ux−32​t​vx​ux2−t​Dx​(u​v)​ux​x\displaystyle\quad\,\,\,=u\,v+t\,u\,v\,u_{x}-\frac{3}{2}\,t\,v_{x}u_{x}^{2}-t\,D_{x}\left(u\,v\right)u_{xx}
+Dx​(t​u​v​ux​x+32​t​v​ux2).\displaystyle\qquad\,+\,D_{x}\left(t\,u\,v\,u_{xx}+\frac{3}{2}\,t\,v\,u_{x}^{2}\right). (36)

We can shift the last term in Eq. (36) into C2C^{2} by using the identity

Dt​(C~1+Dx​(A))+Dx​(C2)=Dt​(C~1)+Dx​(C2+Dt​(A))D_{t}({\tilde{C}}^{1}+D_{x}(A))+D_{x}(C^{2})=D_{t}({\tilde{C}}^{1})+D_{x}(C^{2}+D_{t}(A))

and obtain

C1=u​v+t​u​v​ux−32​t​vx​ux2−t​Dx​(u​v)​ux​x.C^{1}=u\,v+t\,u\,v\,u_{x}-\frac{3}{2}\,t\,v_{x}u_{x}^{2}-t\,D_{x}\left(u\,v\right)u_{xx}. (37)

Now we substitute in Eq. (37) the expression (30) for vv, shift the terms of the form Dx​(⋯)D_{x}(\cdots) into C2C^{2} and finally arrive at the conserved vector with the following components:

C1=a​u+b​u3,C2=−a⁡(12​u2+ux2+u​ux​x)−b⁡(34​u4+3​u3​ux​x).\begin{split}&C^{1}=a\,u+b\,u^{3},\\[6.45831pt] &C^{2}=-a\left(\frac{1}{2}\,u^{2}+u_{x}^{2}+u\,u_{xx}\right)-b\left(\frac{3}{4}\,u^{4}+3\,u^{3}\,u_{xx}\right).\end{split} (38)

The vector (38) is a linear combination with constant coefficients aa and bb of the following two linearly independent conserved vectors:

C1=u,C2=−12​u2−ux2−u​ux​xC^{1}=u,\,\,\qquad C^{2}=-\frac{1}{2}\,u^{2}-u_{x}^{2}-u\,u_{xx} (39)

and

C1=u3,C2=−34​u4−3​u3​ux​x.C^{1}=u^{3},\qquad C^{2}=-\frac{3}{4}\,u^{4}-3\,u^{3}\,u_{xx}. (40)

The conservation equation (25) for the vector (39) coincides with Eq. (28), whereas the vector (40) provides a new conservation law for the Rosenau-Hyman equation.

3.3 Camassa-Holm equation

For the Camassa-Holm equation (1) the formal Lagrangian (24) is written

ℒ=v⁡[ut−13​(ut​x​x+ux​t​x+ux​x​t)−u​ux​x​x−2​ux​ux​x+3​u​ux+κ​ux].{\cal{L}}=v\left[u_{t}-\frac{1}{3}(u_{txx}+u_{xtx}+u_{xxt})-uu_{xxx}-2\,u_{x}u_{xx}+3\,uu_{x}+\kappa\,u_{x}\right]. (41)

We will construct the conservation law by taking the substitution (22) of the particular form v=uv=u. We use the following symmetry of Eq. (1):

X=−2t∂∂t+κt∂∂x+(κ+2u)∂∂u⋅X=-2\,t\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\kappa\,t\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+\left(\kappa+2\,u\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\,\cdot (42)

Proceeding as in Section 3.2, we obtain the following conserved vector associated with the symmetry (42):

C1=2​(u2+ux2)+κ​u,C2=4​(u3−u2​ux​x−u​ut​x)+κ⁡(72​u2−12​ux2−u​ux​x−ut​x+κ​u).\begin{split}&C^{1}=2(u^{2}+u_{x}^{2})+\kappa\,u,\\[6.45831pt] &C^{2}=4(u^{3}-u^{2}\,u_{xx}-u\,u_{tx})+\kappa\left(\frac{7}{2}\,u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,u_{x}^{2}-u\,u_{xx}-u_{tx}+\kappa\,u\right).\end{split} (43)

When κ=0\kappa=0 in Eq. (1) the symmetry (42) takes the form (31), and the conserved vector (43) becomes

C1=u2+ux2,C2=2​(u3−u2​ux​x−u​ut​x).C^{1}=u^{2}+u_{x}^{2},\qquad C^{2}=2\left(u^{3}-u^{2}u_{xx}-u\,u_{tx}\right). (44)

It is shown in [1] that the well known infinite series of conservation laws of the KdV equation can be obtained by applying the formulae (27) to the infinite set of Lie-Bäcklund and non-local symmetries of the KdV equation. The similar procedure can be applied to the Camassa-Holm and Rosenau-Hyman equations. This is a topic for further research.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
